description: A private journal, with a thoughtful reflection after every entry.
lead: A quiet place for reflection, drawing on a deep philosophical tradition.

points.title: A few lines are enough
points.text: The benefit of journaling comes from reflecting each day. A prompt is there when the page feels blank.

points.title: A well-stocked library of traditional wisdom
points.text: Reflections draw only on {works} chosen works, from Plato and the Stoics to William James, and tell you exactly where to find each passage.

points.title: Easily explore past entries
points.text: Every reflection ends with a question to carry forward. Browse your favorites, search, or explore a theme.

points.title: Private, and never used to train AI
points.text: Entries are encrypted with a passphrase only you know, and are never used to train AI.

reminder_prompts: What's one thing you're carrying into today?
What went well this week, and what part did you play in it?
What's within your control today, and what isn't?
What's been on your mind when things go quiet?
Who has been on your mind lately, and why?
What are you grateful for this morning?
Where do you need patience right now?
What would make today a good day, by your own measure?
What has been hard lately, and what has helped?
What's one habit you'd like to strengthen?
What have you learned about yourself recently?
What's a small kindness you could offer someone today?

sample.title: Ten quiet minutes
sample.entry: I wanted ten quiet minutes with my coffee before everyone got up, but I checked my phone "just for a second" and the whole day came flooding in: the meeting at ten, a bill I forgot, an email I haven't answered. The coffee went cold. I'd like my mornings to feel like mine again, not like the first item on the list.
paragraphs: You describe the phone as an intruder that broke into your ten minutes. I'd ask whether it was more of an exit. Pascal made a famous diagnosis: “all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.” He wasn't talking about villains or addicts. He meant ordinary people who reach for something, anything, when the quiet starts to feel a little exposed.

Notice what "just for a second" was probably doing. The meeting, the bill, and the email were already in your head before you picked up the phone. In stillness, they were going to surface anyway. The phone let you meet them as tasks, which feels busy and productive, instead of as a mood, which feels like sitting with unease. Pascal's sharper point is that we chase the hunt rather than the hare. Checking can feel like relief even when it produces none.

So guarding the ten minutes may take more than moving the phone to another room, though that helps. It may mean letting the list show up in your mind and not answering it yet. The quiet was never empty. It was crowded, and the phone only made the crowd official. What would it take to let those items stand there while your coffee is still hot?
sample.question: When your hand went to the phone, what did you feel in the seconds just before, and what were you hoping the screen would give you?
sample.note: A real reflection from A Life Well Lived, as it was written.

welcome_quote.text: “The unexamined life is not worth living.”

writers.name: Plato
writers.label: Socrates and Plato
writers.guide: the examined life; knowing that you don't know; questioning what a word like "fair" or "success" really means; the harmony of reason, spirit and appetite in the soul; the cave, and mistaking shadows for reality; love as a longing that can lead upward.

writers.name: Aristotle
writers.guide: virtue as a mean between extremes; character formed by habit ("we become just by doing just acts"); eudaimonia as flourishing activity, not a feeling; practical wisdom; friendship and its kinds.

writers.name: Epicurus
writers.guide: pleasure as the absence of pain and anxiety, not indulgence; sorting desires into natural and necessary, natural but unnecessary, and empty; "death is nothing to us"; friendship as the greatest support of a happy life; the quiet, simple life.

writers.name: Cicero
writers.guide: old age as a season with its own work and pleasures; facing death without fear; grief and other "disturbances" as judgments that philosophy can treat; whether virtue alone is enough for a happy life; duty and public life.

writers.name: Seneca
writers.guide: time as the one thing truly ours, and how much of it we give away; premeditatio malorum, rehearsing what might go wrong; anger as a short madness.

writers.name: Epictetus
writers.guide: the dichotomy of control, what is up to us and what isn't; judgments versus events, being disturbed not by things but by our view of them.

writers.name: Marcus Aurelius
writers.guide: the view from above; amor fati, welcoming what happens as part of the whole; doing the work in front of you without complaint or applause.

writers.name: Lucretius
writers.guide: freedom from fear through understanding nature; death as nothing to be afraid of; the restlessness of people fleeing themselves; watching the storm from the shore.

writers.name: Plutarch
writers.guide: practical ethics: contentedness of mind, restraining anger, telling a flatterer from a friend, noticing your own progress, curiosity and talkativeness.

writers.name: Augustine
writers.era: Late antiquity and the Middle Ages
writers.guide: the restless heart; disordered loves, wanting good things in the wrong order; memory and the self; the will divided against itself.

writers.name: Boethius
writers.era: Late antiquity and the Middle Ages
writers.guide: consolation in loss; Fortune's wheel, and how anything Fortune gives she can take back; false goods (wealth, fame, power, pleasure) against true happiness; whether misfortune teaches more than good luck; freedom and providence.

writers.name: Anselm of Canterbury
writers.era: Late antiquity and the Middle Ages
writers.guide: "faith seeking understanding", and "I believe in order to understand", as a stance toward any commitment you can't fully prove; longing and searching as part of finding; the idea of that than which nothing greater can be conceived.

writers.name: Thomas Aquinas
writers.era: Late antiquity and the Middle Ages
writers.guide: virtues as stable dispositions built by practice; the passions as raw material that reason can shape.

writers.name: Dante Alighieri
writers.era: Late antiquity and the Middle Ages
writers.guide: being lost "midway upon the journey of our life"; sins that become their own punishment; change as a slow climb rather than a single decision; love as the root of every virtue and every fault, when it is misdirected, too weak or excessive; contentment in accepting one's place.

writers.name: Michel de Montaigne
writers.guide: studying yourself honestly, contradictions included; "What do I know?"; how much of what we call reason is custom; friendship; solitude and keeping a room of one's own in the mind; making peace with death, the body and an ordinary life.

writers.name: Francis Bacon
writers.guide: short, dense counsel on conduct: what studies are for; revenge and letting it go; envy; friendship as the halving of griefs; adversity as the test of virtue.

writers.name: René Descartes
writers.guide: radical doubt, rebuilding from what you can be sure of; provisional rules for acting while uncertain.

writers.name: Blaise Pascal
writers.guide: diversion, and our inability to sit quietly alone in a room; the restlessness behind busyness; the grandeur and wretchedness of being human; vanity and self-love; the wager, choosing how to live without certainty.

writers.name: François de La Rochefoucauld
writers.guide: self-love behind our virtues; vanity; the ways we deceive ourselves and call it something better.
writers.caution: Use one maxim to test a motive, never to conclude that every motive is false.

writers.name: Baruch Spinoza
writers.guide: emotions as confused ideas; freedom as understanding their causes; bondage to the passions.

writers.name: John Locke
writers.guide: personal identity and consciousness: what makes you the same person over time.

writers.name: David Hume
writers.guide: reason as "the slave of the passions"; habit and custom; the self as a bundle of perceptions.

writers.name: Adam Smith
writers.guide: sympathy as the root of moral judgment; the impartial spectator within, by whose eyes we judge our own conduct; wanting to be praiseworthy and not merely praised; how admiring wealth and rank misleads us.

writers.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
writers.guide: telling the truth about yourself, shame included; the gap between how we are and how we wish to appear; living in other people's eyes; solitude and nature.
writers.caution: For honesty about oneself, not as a model of conduct.

writers.name: Immanuel Kant
writers.guide: acting from duty rather than inclination; treating people (yourself included) as ends, never merely as means; whether you could will your maxim as a universal law; autonomy as self-legislation.

writers.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
writers.guide: what we are matters more to happiness than what we have or how we seem; aiming at freedom from pain rather than at pleasure; self-sufficiency and solitude; the restless wanting of the will.
writers.caution: His practical counsel only; never press his pessimism on someone who is struggling.

writers.name: Søren Kierkegaard
writers.guide: choosing yourself, and the leap you can't reason your way into; the aesthetic life of moods and pleasures against the ethical life of commitment; anxiety and despair as signs of a self not yet chosen; Abraham and faith beyond what can be explained; becoming a single individual instead of hiding in "the crowd".

writers.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
writers.guide: trusting your own thought against conformity; compensation, every gain having its price; character over reputation; friendship; circles, every end a beginning.

writers.name: Henry David Thoreau
writers.guide: living deliberately; the real cost of a thing as the amount of life exchanged for it; simplicity; solitude; stepping to the music you hear.

writers.name: John Stuart Mill
writers.guide: happiness as the measure of right action, and higher pleasures over lower ones ("better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied"); liberty, and the harm principle; individuality and "experiments of living"; the danger of conformity and custom; truth emerging from honest disagreement.

writers.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
writers.guide: asking where your values come from and what they serve; self-overcoming; saying yes to your own life; suspicion of resentment dressed up as virtue.
writers.caution: Use him to unsettle a comfortable assumption, never to excuse contempt for others or to belittle compassion or faith.

writers.name: William James
writers.guide: habit as the flywheel of character, and how new habits are made; choosing to believe where evidence cannot decide; the divided self and its healing; what makes a life significant; our blindness to other people's inner lives.

writers.name: Viktor Frankl
writers.works: Man's Search for Meaning, The Doctor and the Soul
writers.guide: meaning as the deepest human need; the last freedom, choosing one's attitude in any circumstances; meaning found in work, in love and in how unavoidable suffering is borne.

writers.name: Albert Camus
writers.works: The Myth of Sisyphus, The Plague, The Rebel
writers.guide: the absurd, the gap between our need for meaning and the world's silence; revolt, living fully and lucidly without appeal; decency and solidarity in the face of suffering.
writers.caution: The Myth of Sisyphus opens with the question of suicide: never bring that theme to someone who is struggling.

writers.name: Hannah Arendt
writers.works: The Human Condition, Eichmann in Jerusalem, The Life of the Mind
writers.guide: thinking as a silent dialogue with yourself; wrong done through thoughtlessness rather than malice; labor, work and action; the capacity to begin something new; forgiving and promising as remedies for what can't be undone or foreseen.

sources_intro: Reflections quote only the works below, each in a public-domain translation (or original English edition) on Wikisource or Project Gutenberg. Every quotation is checked word for word against that text before you see it, and links to the passage it came from.

source_groups.name: Classical Greece
source_groups.about: Athens, from the 5th to the 3rd century BC, where the examined life began. Socrates wrote nothing; his words come to us through Plato's dialogues.

source_groups.name: Rome and the Stoics
source_groups.about: Cicero, and the Stoics Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius: philosophy as a practice for living, in good fortune and bad.

source_groups.name: Late antiquity and the Middle Ages
source_groups.about: Faith and reason together: from Augustine and Boethius to Anselm, Aquinas and Dante.

source_groups.name: Early modern philosophy
source_groups.about: The 17th and 18th centuries: doubt, reason, the passions and the self.

source_groups.name: Modern philosophy
source_groups.about: Duty, freedom and the single individual: Kant, Kierkegaard and Mill.

paraphrase_only.about: These writers are still in copyright, so reflections may draw on their ideas in their own words, naming the writer and book, but never quote them, and there are no links.
